reservoir

/REZ-er-vwahr/ - the stress falls on REZ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Reservoir means a large stored supply or reserve.

A camel's hump is a reservoir of fat — energy banked against the lean weeks.

Example

The regional blood bank keeps a reservoir of O-negative behind a steel door: pint after pint, built up through slow Tuesday drives, for the one night a crash arrives and there is no time to type a patient. Most weeks the door barely opens. That is the point of it.

Reservoir is the exact word because the supply is stored against future need — built up in calm, drawn on in crisis. A pile merely sits; a stash merely hides. A reservoir is kept, the way its Latin root promises: something held back on purpose, waiting to be needed.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cache: A cache is a store tucked out of sight until it is wanted — small, hidden, and found again only by whoever hid it. A reservoir needs no secrecy: it is deep, often shared, and drawn on steadily over time. Concealment makes the cache; depth and steady reuse make the reservoir.

hoard: A hoard is a store guarded for the keeping's own sake — the dragon's gold, gloated over rather than spent. A reservoir is kept in order to be used: built up in calm, drawn down in need, refilled after. Hoarding is about clinging; a reservoir is about being ready.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

shortage: not enough to go around

drought: a supply gone dry — of water or of anything else

Where it sits · how deep and lasting the supply runs

stash → stockpile → reservoir

stash vs. reservoir: A stash is small and personal — candy behind the cookbooks; a reservoir holds a community's worth, deep enough to draw on for years.

stockpile vs. reservoir: A stockpile is big and built on purpose, but it is counted in crates; a reservoir goes a rung further — a depth you draw on steadily and refill, more well than warehouse.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: back

Root — serv-: to keep, guard (Latin servare)

Suffix — -oir: place for (French)

Put it together: Re- (back) + serv- (to keep, guard — Latin servare) + -oir (a place for) = a place where things are kept back. French réservoir named the holding basin; English borrowed the basin and then let it hold anything — water, blood, patience, goodwill — so long as it is stored against need.

Use the root in a new word: conserve: Rangers asked hikers to conserve water until the springs ran again.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / figurative

Reservoir began as the water word and now stores anything drawn on over time — patience, goodwill, facts. Its shelf-mates are sized differently: a cache is tucked out of sight, a stockpile is counted in crates, a reservoir is deep and refillable. Beware the sound-alike reservation (a booking, or a doubt): you draw on a reservoir; you make a reservation.
